sections.text:
What next? Our opponents are certainly well supplied with arguments. “We are baptized into water,” they say. “Surely, then, we shall not honor water above all creation or give it a share in the honor of the Father and the Son.”

Such arguments are what one expects from angry disputants who leave no method untried against the person who has offended them, their reasoning clouded by passion. Yet we will not avoid the discussion. Even if we do not succeed in teaching those who do not know, at least we shall not retreat before those who act maliciously.

Let us therefore go back for a moment to the beginning of the matter.

The economy of our God and Savior concerning humanity is a recall from the fall and a return from the alienation caused by disobedience into intimacy with God. For this reason came Christ's sojourn in the flesh, the pattern of life described in the Gospels, the sufferings, the cross, the tomb, and the resurrection: so that the person being saved through imitation of Christ might recover the ancient adoption.

For the perfection of life, imitation of Christ is necessary—not only imitation of the gentleness, humility, and endurance shown in his life, but imitation even of his death. Paul, imitator of Christ, says that he is “being conformed to his death, if somehow I may attain the resurrection from the dead.”

How, then, are we made in the likeness of his death? By being buried with him through baptism. What is this burial, and what advantage comes from imitating it?

First the continuity of the old life must be cut off. This is impossible unless one is born again, according to the Lord's word. Regeneration, as the very name shows, is the beginning of a second life. Before the second life begins, therefore, the first must reach its end. Just as runners turning at the end of a course pause between movements in opposite directions, so in the change of lives death stands between the two, bringing the former life to an end and beginning the life that follows.

How do we accomplish the descent into death? By imitating Christ's burial through baptism. The bodies of those baptized are in a manner buried in water. Baptism therefore signifies sacramentally the putting away of the works of the flesh, as the Apostle says: “You were circumcised with a circumcision not made by hands, in the putting off of the body of the flesh, in the circumcision of Christ, having been buried with him in baptism.”

There is also a cleansing of the soul from the stain accumulated through the mind set on the flesh, as it is written: “Wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow.” For this reason we do not wash repeatedly at every defilement according to Jewish ritual practice, but confess one saving baptism. There is one death on behalf of the world and one resurrection from the dead, and baptism is their type.

For this reason the Lord, dispenser of our life, gave us the covenant of baptism containing the image of death and life: water fulfills the figure of death, while the Spirit supplies the pledge of life.

Thus the reason why water is joined with the Spirit becomes clear. In baptism two ends are set before us: the destruction of the body of sin so that it no longer bears fruit for death, and life in the Spirit so that our fruit may be holiness. Water receives the body as though into a tomb and represents death; the Spirit pours in life-giving power, renewing our souls from the deadness of sin to their original life.

This is what it means to be born again of water and Spirit: death is enacted in the water, while life is worked in us through the Spirit.

The great mystery of baptism is completed in three immersions and three invocations, so that the figure of death may be fully represented and the souls of the baptized enlightened through the tradition of divine knowledge. If there is grace in the water, it comes not from the nature of the water but from the presence of the Spirit. Baptism is “not the removal of dirt from the flesh, but the appeal of a good conscience toward God.”

Preparing us for the life that follows the resurrection, the Lord sets before us the whole evangelical manner of life: gentleness, endurance under wrong, freedom from the pollution of pleasure and from greed, so that by deliberate choice we may already accomplish beforehand what the coming life possesses naturally.

If, then, someone defined the Gospel as a preliminary sketch of the life after the resurrection, I would not judge the definition to go beyond what is fitting. But let us return to the subject.

Through the Holy Spirit comes our restoration to paradise, our ascent into the kingdom of heaven, our return to the adoption of children, our freedom to call God our Father, our participation in the grace of Christ, our being called children of light, our sharing in eternal glory, and—in a word—our being brought into the fullness of every blessing, both in this age and in the age to come.

The good things stored up for us in promise are already contemplated by faith as though present, while we await their full enjoyment. If such is the pledge, what must the perfection be? If such are the firstfruits, what will the complete fulfillment be?

The difference between the grace of the Spirit and baptism with water can also be grasped from this: John baptized with water, but our Lord Jesus Christ baptizes in the Holy Spirit. “I baptize you in water for repentance, but the One coming after me is stronger than I, whose sandals I am not worthy to carry; he will baptize you in the Holy Spirit and fire.”

Here the trial of judgment is called baptism of fire, as the Apostle says: “The fire will test each one's work, what sort it is”; and again, “the Day will reveal it, because it is revealed in fire.”

Some who contended for true religion have even undergone death for Christ not merely in symbol but in fact and therefore needed no outward sign of water for salvation, because they were baptized in their own blood.

I say this not to diminish baptism in water but to overthrow the arguments of those who exalt themselves against the Spirit, confusing realities that are distinct and comparing things that cannot rightly be compared.

translator_notes: The chapter presents baptism as participation in Christ's death and resurrection and distinguishes the sign of water from the life-giving operation of the Spirit.
Basil explicitly witnesses triple immersion and triple invocation in the baptismal rite.
The closing reference to martyrdom reflects the ancient doctrine commonly called baptism of blood.
